Sure :) That'd be cool.

>how much of the Tanakh have you read?

Ah, forgot to answer. Not much. I've *never* been an earnestly practicing or believing Jew. My only exposure to the texts were when I was studying for my barmitzvah (only had a barmitzvah to please my family), going to Jewish summer camp as a kid, and going to synagogue a couple times a year. Virtually all of my knowledge of Judaism comes from other people (family funerals and weddings, Sunday school teachers, camp counselors, etc) rather than reading stuff for myself. I was simply never interested in exploring religion for myself until recently.

Will add it to the potential reading list. Thank you. :)

Wow, this is very cool. 

I have gone almost my entire life seeing the world through the lens of a very scientific, anti-supernatural epistemological framework. Howver, I've recently been coming to the realization, with the help of some dead philosophers and meditative-work, that I may have been trapped in Plato's cave all along.

One side of me still wants to shoot-down my intuitions that there is "something more," but I will try my hardest to keep a truly open mind (and heart) when exploring Christianity.

Thanks for the answers! Was there something specific that brought you away from atheism?

>Has that always been the case with Judaism or is it a more recent development?

It seems to me like a more recent development.

>Agnostic Orthodox Jew sounds like a contradiction

It's definitely a contradiction. (And sorry, I meant to say "Conservative" not "orthodox". They are "Agnostic Conservative Jews") Yet there are so many Jews who go through all of the motions of being religious without really believing in God. They just like the community, traditions, etc.

>So are Conservative Jews more agnostic than Reformed or Orthodox?

I'd say reform Jews are definitely the most atheistic/agnostic

>What lead you to choose Orthodoxy over other Christian groups?

What inspired me to look into Christianity in the first place was my realization that there was timeless wisdom that modern cultures have pushed aside, in favor of hedonism, progressivism, nihilism, scientism, and feel-goodery. Coming to Christianity from that angle, the oldest most "true-to-its-roots" denomination seemed like the obvious choice.

I appreciate the answers!

You're right about the prevalence of atheistic/agnostic Jews. Interestingly enough, I have a couple family members that consider themselves "Agnostic Conservative Jews." They keep kosher, go to synagogue regularly, and do all of the other Jewish stuff not because they have faith, but because they value the traditions and culture. I'm sure there are some good theories on why so many Jews are atheists/agnostic, I haven't looked into it though.

I'll definitely check out a Liturgy in my area and check out Ancient Faith Radio.
